en: The Scripture on the Divination of the Retribution of Good and Evil Karma, Volume One, excerpted from the *Ṣaḍindriyasaṃgraha-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhidīpa of Central India.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān, the Omniscient One, was staying in the city of Rājagṛha.

On Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, by means of his supernormal powers, he manifested a vast, magnificent, pure, and unobstructed site of enlightenment; there, together with an immeasurable and boundless great assembly, he expounded the profound Dharma-door of the *mūla-skandha*.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Firm Pure Faith. He rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now wish to ask a question within this assembly and seek counsel from the World-Honored One; I pray that you will deign to grant me your permission to hear."
The Buddha said,
“Good son, you may speak according to whatever you wish to ask.”
The Bodhisattva Firm Pure Faith said:
"As the Buddha previously stated:
'If, after I have passed away, the True Dharma has been extinguished, the Semblance Dharma is nearing its end, and one enters the Final Age.'"

At such a time, sentient beings have meager merit and are beset by many forms of decline and affliction; the lands are frequently in turmoil, calamities arise repeatedly, and they are oppressed and disturbed by various misfortunes and fears.
My disciples have lost their wholesome mindfulness; they only increase greed, anger, jealousy, and pride.

Even if some among them appear to practice the wholesome Dharma, they do so merely to seek worldly gain and fame, making these their primary concern, and are thus unable to single-mindedly cultivate the Dharma of transcendence.

At that time, sentient beings beheld the calamities and chaos of the world; their minds were constantly timid and weak, filled with anxiety and fear that they and their kinsmen would not obtain food and clothing to sustain their lives.
Due to such numerous causes and conditions of obstruction, those within the Buddha-dharma who possess dull faculties and little faith are many, while those who attain the Way are extremely few.
Even gradually, among those of the three vehicles, those who achieve the perfection of faith are likewise exceedingly rare.

All those who had practiced worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*), developed the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā-karma*), and attained knowledge of their own past lives, subsequently ceased to exist.

Thus, later on, after a long period within the *mappō* (degenerate dharma) age, there was a total absence of anyone who had attained the Way, gained faith, or achieved meditative concentration, supernormal powers, and so forth.

"I now ask the Tathāgata on behalf of those in the future evil age, during the period when the Semblance Dharma is nearing its end and within the Final Dharma, who possess even a slight root of goodness."
By what skillful means can they be opened, transformed, instructed, and guided, so that they may give rise to faith and eliminate their decline and afflictions?
Because those sentient beings encounter an evil age and face many obstacles, their wholesome minds regress.

Within the laws of cause and effect pertaining to both the mundane and supramundane realms, they repeatedly give rise to doubt and are unable to seek the wholesome Dharma with a firm and focused mind.
Such sentient beings are pitiable and worthy of salvation.
World-Honored One of great compassion and omniscience!
We pray that you will employ skillful means to instruct and enlighten us,
so that we may leave the net of doubt behind, eliminate all obstacles, and cause our faith to increase.
"Whichever vehicle one follows, one will swiftly attain non-retrogression.
The Buddha said to Dṛḍhaśraddhā: "Excellent!"
Excellent! It is well that you ask about this matter; it deeply accords with my own intention.
Within this assembly, there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Kṣitigarbha; you should inquire about this matter of him.
"He shall establish skillful means for you, revealing and expounding them so as to fulfill your aspiration.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Firm Pure Faith addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Tathāgata, World-Honored One, Supreme Unsurpassed Wisdom!"
"With what intention do you not speak yourself, but instead wish for the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha to expound it?
The Buddha told Dṛḍhaprasāda:
"Do not give rise to thoughts of superiority or inferiority."

Since this son of good family first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed; he has long since been able to cross the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), and his merits are fully perfected.
However, by virtue of the sovereign power of his original vows, he manifests through skillful means and transformations, responding like reflections throughout the ten directions.

Although he universally traverses all buddha-lands and constantly initiates meritorious deeds, his transformative benefits are particularly profound in the world of the five turbidities; this is because it is perfumed by the power of his original vows and because sentient beings possess the karmic conditions to receive his transformation.
For eleven kalpas, he has adorned this world and brought sentient beings to maturity.
Therefore, within this assembly, his physical form is dignified and majestic, and his spiritual power is preeminent; with the exception of the Tathāgata, there is no one who can surpass him.
Furthermore, regarding all transformative activities within this world, none can equal those of the great Bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra and Avalokiteśvara.

By the power of these Bodhisattvas' original vows, they swiftly fulfill all the requests of sentient beings, are able to extinguish all their grave offenses, eliminate all obstacles, and bring about immediate peace and security.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva is called one who skillfully provides consolation and instruction.
That is to say, he is adept at expounding the profound Dharma and is able to skillfully guide beginners who have resolved to seek the Mahāyāna, ensuring they do not become discouraged or weak.
For these and other such reasons, sentient beings in this world yearn with thirsting longing, receiving transformation and attaining deliverance.
Therefore, I now cause him to speak it.
At that time, having understood the Buddha’s intention, the Bodhisattva Firm Pure Faith immediately exhorted the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha, saying:
“Excellent, O True Being who saves the world!
Excellent, O Bodhisattva of Great Wisdom! As I have asked:
"By what skillful means should one transform and guide the sentient beings of the evil age, so that they may be freed from all obstacles and attain firm faith?"
"The Tathāgata now wishes to have you explain these skillful means.
You should know the proper time; out of compassion, please speak for us.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dṛḍhaśuddhādhimukti, saying:
“Good son! Listen attentively.
I shall explain it for you.”

If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in this degenerate age, there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who have not attained decisive faith in the laws of cause and effect regarding the mundane and supramundane; who are unable to cultivate and bring to realization the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, and the perception of impurity;
who are unable to diligently contemplate the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
and who likewise do not diligently contemplate such dharmas as True Suchness (tathatā), the Reality Limit (bhūtakoṭi), and the absence of arising and ceasing.
Because they do not diligently contemplate such dharmas, they are unable to ultimately refrain from the fundamental transgressions of the ten unwholesome paths of action.
They are unable to maintain exclusive faith in the various spheres of the merits of the Triple Gem.
Within the three vehicles, none have a fixed direction.
For such persons, if there are various obstructing matters that increase their anxiety, or if they experience doubt or regret, their minds will not be clear in any respect.
Excessive seeking leads to much affliction; one is entangled by numerous affairs, one’s actions become unstable, and the mind is disturbed, thereby causing the abandonment of the practice of the Way.

For those who encounter such obstacles and difficulties, they should employ the method of the wooden wheel signs to divinate the good and evil karma of past lives, as well as present matters of suffering and happiness, fortune and misfortune.
Existence arises through the conjunction of conditions; when conditions cease, it is extinguished.
Karma accumulates according to the mind, and as its characteristics manifest, the fruit arises.
It is neither lost nor destroyed; it corresponds without deviation.
Thus, by accurately divining the retribution of good and evil karma and instructing one’s own mind,
one may reach a definitive understanding regarding matters of doubt.
If a disciple of the Buddha merely studies such methods of divination and takes refuge with a sincere heart, there will be nothing among the matters observed that is not true and authentic.

One should not abandon such teachings as these, only to pursue worldly divination, various signs of good and bad fortune, and other such matters, becoming greedily attached to and delighting in their practice.
If one delights in practicing this, it will deeply obstruct the Noble Path. "Good son!

One who wishes to learn the characteristics of the wooden wheel should first carve a piece of wood about the size of a little finger, making its length less than one inch. The center should be made square and level on all four sides, while the rest of the wood is gradually tapered away toward both ends."
When held with the palm facing upward and cast aside, it is made to turn easily; for this reason, it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*).

Furthermore, based on these characteristics, it can destroy the net of false views and doubts of sentient beings, turning them toward the right path and leading them to a place of peace and security; therefore, it is named a "wheel."
Regarding the characteristics of these wheels, there are three types of distinctions. What are the three?
First, the wheel characteristics can demonstrate the distinctions among the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma performed in past lives; these wheels are ten in number.

Second, the wheel-sign can demonstrate the duration—whether long or short—of karma accumulated in past lives, as well as the distinctions of its strength, weakness, magnitude, and smallness; this wheel has three [sections].
Third, the wheel-sign can demonstrate the distinctions in the retribution received throughout the three periods of time; this wheel has six [sections].
"If one wishes to observe the distinctions between the wholesome and unwholesome karmas performed in past lives, one should carve wood into ten wheels.
Based upon these ten wheels, one should record the names of the ten wholesome actions."
First, place the ten wholesome deeds on one wheel and record them on one side.
Next, write the ten unwholesome deeds opposite the ten wholesome deeds so that they correspond, and likewise record each set on its own side.
The so-called ten wholesome actions constitute the root of all wholesome dharmas and are able to encompass all other wholesome dharmas.
The so-called ten unwholesome actions likewise constitute the root of all unwholesome dharmas and are able to encompass all other unwholesome dharmas.
"If one wishes to perform divination using this wheel-mandala, one should first train in wholeheartedly prostrating to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
Thereupon, one should make this vow:
'May all sentient beings of the ten directions swiftly attain the opportunity to draw near to, make offerings to, and receive instruction in the True Dharma from them.'"
Next, one should learn to pay homage with a sincere heart to all the treasuries of the Dharma throughout the ten directions.
Thereupon, one should establish this vow:

"May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions swiftly attain the ability to receive, uphold, read, and recite [the teachings], practice them according to the Dharma, and explain them to others."
Next, one should learn to reverently prostrate with a sincere heart to all the worthy and holy ones of the ten directions.
Thereupon, one should immediately establish this vow:

"May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions swiftly attain the opportunity to draw near to and make offerings to them, resolve to attain Bodhicitta, and remain firm in their purpose without ever regressing."
"Later, you should learn to pay homage to me, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha, with a sincere mind.
You should then make this vow:
'May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions swiftly eliminate their heavy karmic offenses and evil deeds, and be freed from all obstacles.'"
"May all necessities of life be fully provided.
Having performed such prostrations, one should offer whatever incense, flowers, and so forth are available. Regarding the practice of making offerings:
one should look up with mindfulness toward the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, whose essence is eternally pervasive and omnipresent.
May these incense and flowers be equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), universally perfuming all Buddha-fields and performing the work of Buddhas.
Furthermore, one should contemplate that all offerings throughout the ten directions exist at all times.

I shall now, by means of all the various kinds of incense, flowers, necklaces, banners, pennants, precious canopies, and all manner of exquisite ornaments; by means of various kinds of music, lamps, candles, food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine; and even by means of all the various implements for adornment and offering existing throughout the ten directions—recalling and mentally representing these from afar—universally offer and present them as an act of worship together with all sentient beings.
I should reflect that among all worlds there are those who practice making offerings, and I now rejoice in them.
As for those who have not yet practiced making offerings, may they be inspired and guided so that they may come to practice making offerings.

Furthermore, may my body swiftly reach all buddha-fields, and at the abodes of all Buddhas, Dharmas, and Saṅghas, may I, together with all sentient beings, equally offer and present every kind of adorned article of worship.

I shall make offerings to all Buddhas’ Dharma-bodies, form-bodies, relics, images, stupas, and shrines—all such Buddha-works; I shall make offerings to all treasuries of the Dharma and all places where the Dharma is preached; I shall make offerings to all the assemblies of noble and holy Sangha. Together with all sentient beings, having performed such offerings and practiced them, may we gradually achieve the six pāramitās and the four immeasurable minds.
They deeply realize that all phenomena are originally quiescent, neither arising nor ceasing, of one flavor and equality, pure and free from conceptualization, and ultimately perfect.
Furthermore, you should separately and repeatedly fix your mind to make offerings to me, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha.
Next, you should recite my name, either silently or aloud,
and address me with single-minded devotion, saying:
"Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha.
Reciting this name in this manner until it is completed a thousand times,
and having performed these thousand recitations, one speaks these words:
“Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva Mahasattva!
Greatly Compassionate One!
We only pray that you will protect and mind us and all sentient beings, swiftly eliminating all obstacles, increasing pure faith, and causing what we now observe to correspond with reality.”
Having spoken these words, he then took a wooden wheel in his hand and cast it sideways upon a clean surface.
In this same manner, whether one wishes to examine oneself or to examine another, it is done in exactly this way.
"One should know that in interpreting the marks of the wheel, one must carefully observe and verify each manifestation according to the karma it reveals—

whether it be purely endowed with the ten wholesome actions, purely endowed with the ten unwholesome actions, a mixture of good and evil, purely wholesome but incomplete, or purely unwholesome but incomplete."
Such karmic causes differ in their types; the fruits of their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are each distinct, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has explained extensively elsewhere.

One should recollect, contemplate, and examine the manifested seeds of karma to see whether they correspond to the experiences of suffering, pleasure, fortune, or misfortune resulting from the retribution of this present life. That which accords with them is called "correspondence" (*saṃprayukta*);
that which does not accord is said to be due to a lack of sincerity, termed "error" (*vibhrama*).

"If, when examining the marks of the wheels, neither their good nor evil karma appears, it means this person has already realized the mind of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). Being solely intent on seeking liberation, they no longer delight in receiving worldly retributions; thus, all tainted karmas (*sāsrava-karma*) become progressively weaker and no longer increase, which is why they do not appear."

Furthermore, regarding those who possess neither pure goodness nor pure evil: for these two types of persons, whatever karmic actions of good or evil do not manifest are all weak and unable to draw forth their results; therefore, they do not appear.

If, in future ages, the disciples of the Buddha have already determined that their good and evil karmic retributions correspond to their actions, and they encounter objects of the five desires that accord with their wishes, they must not indulge themselves or give rise to negligence.
One should then reflect:
"It is because of such virtuous karma from my past lives that I have now obtained this retribution.
I should now further advance in my cultivation and must not cease."

If one encounters various calamities, diverse forms of decay and affliction, or inauspicious events that cause disturbance, anxiety, and fear, or when things do not go as desired, one should accept them with equanimity; one must not harbor doubt or regret, nor withdraw from the cultivation of wholesome deeds.
One should then reflect:

"It is solely because I created such evil karma in my past lives that I now receive this retribution; I must now repent for those evil deeds and single-mindedly cultivate their antidotes as well as other virtues."
"Do not remain in indolence or negligence, for this will only cause you to further accumulate various masses of suffering.
This is called the method for observing the signs of the first wheel. "Good son!

If one wishes to examine and discern the karmic accumulations of the past and former lives—their duration, their strength or weakness, and their distinctions of magnitude—one should further carve wood into three wheels, assigning each to one of the body, speech, and mind, and recording them with written characters.
Furthermore, in the center of the wheel, draw one line on one side, making it thick and long so that it reaches the edge.
Next, draw one line on the second side, making it thin and short so that it does not reach the edge.
Next, on the third face, make a single horizontal incision like a drawing, making it coarse and deep.
Next, on the fourth face, also make a horizontal incision, making it fine and shallow.
One should know that the adornment of wholesome karma is like a painted decoration, while the decay and harm caused by unwholesome karma are like chipping and erosion.

When a painting is large and expansive, it demonstrates that wholesome deeds have been accumulated for a long time, that one's karmic actions were powerful and sharp, and that what was performed was preeminent.
Those carvings that are fine and short indicate that one's accumulation of merit has approached [fruition], yet one’s initial training is dull and what has been accomplished is slight.
Those carvings that are coarse and deep indicate that one has practiced evil for a long time, what has been accomplished is extensive, and the remaining retribution is likewise heavy.

Those carvings that are fine and shallow indicate that one’s wholesome conduct has recently declined and one has begun to practice unwholesome dharmas; the karma thus produced has not yet reached a state of intensity.
Alternatively, it refers to cases where, although grave evil was committed, it has already been repented and amended; this is called "minor evil."

“Good son! If one examines the signs of the first wheel, one may only know the distinctions between the wholesome and unwholesome karma created in past lives, yet one cannot know the duration of their accumulation, nor the strength, weakness, magnitude, or minuteness of the karma performed; therefore, it is necessary to examine the signs of the second wheel.”
If one examines the signs of the second wheel, one should rely on the karma manifested within the signs of the first wheel.
If it pertains to the body, cast the sign of the body wheel;
if it pertains to speech, cast the sign of the speech wheel.
If it pertains to the mind, cast the *cakra* of the mind.
One must not attempt to divine all matters simultaneously with a single throw of these three wheels.
Rather, one should follow the specific mental state of the practitioner and, for each instance of good or evil, cast the divination separately according to the wheel to which it belongs.

"Furthermore, if in the examination of the first wheel-sign one obtains only bodily goodness, yet in this second wheel-sign one obtains bodily evil, this means there was no sincerity of mind and no correspondence; it is termed 'vain error.'"

Furthermore, regarding "inconsistency" (asamyukta): this refers to when, among the signs of the first wheel, one obtains the karma of non-killing and also obtains the karma of stealing; yet, while the mind first focuses on the karma of non-killing, one obtains bodily misconduct within the signs of the second wheel—this is called inconsistency.

"Furthermore, if one observes from birth until the present that one has not delighted in the karma of killing nor committed the transgression of killing, yet the mind was dominated by the intent for the karma of killing, and as a result obtains great physical evil within this second wheel-mark, this is called 'incompatibility' (asamyoga)."
The principle that other actions of speech and mind are not concomitant [with the primary karma] should also be understood in this way. "Good son!

If sentient beings in future ages desire to seek liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death, and first resolve their minds to study and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and signless wisdom (*animitta-prajñā*), they should first contemplate the amount and the gravity of the evil karma they have committed in past lives."
If one's evil karma is abundant and heavy, one cannot immediately study meditative concentration and wisdom; rather, one should first practice the method of repentance. Why is this so?
Because this person’s past habitual tendencies toward an evil mind are so fierce and sharp, they will inevitably commit many evils in the present life and violate the grave prohibitions.

If, having violated these grave prohibitions, they practice meditative concentration and wisdom without first repenting to purify themselves, they will encounter many obstacles and be unable to achieve their goal.
One may lose one's mind and become deranged, be afflicted by external malevolent spirits, or accept false teachings, thereby increasing evil views.

For this reason, one should first practice the method of repentance; if the root of one's precepts is pure and heavy karmic offenses from past lives are rendered slight, then one will be free from all obstacles.
“Good son! One who wishes to practice the dharma of repentance should dwell in a quiet place and, according to one’s ability, adorn a single room.
Within it, one should arrange images of the Buddha and place the scriptures and Dharma; hang silk banners and canopies, and seek out and gather incense and flowers to cultivate offerings.”
Bathe your body and wash your clothes so that they do not become foul or filthy.
During the daytime, remain within this room and recite my name at the three periods of the day.
With single-minded reverence, I pay homage to the seven Buddhas of the past and the fifty-three Buddhas.

Next, following each of the ten directions, I universally take refuge in them all; with focused mind, I prostrate before all the physical bodies, śarīras, images, stūpas, temples, and towers of all Buddhas, as well as all their Buddha-activities.
Next, one should again pay general homage to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

Furthermore, one should direct the mind to pay homage to all treasuries of Dharma throughout the ten directions; next, one should direct the mind to pay homage to all worthy and holy ones throughout the ten directions. Thereafter, one should specifically call upon the names and pay homage to me, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha.
"Having thus paid homage, one should confess the transgressions committed and address them with single-minded devotion:
'I only pray that the Great Compassionate Honored Ones of the ten directions will bear witness, protect, and keep me in mind; I now repent and shall never create [such karma] again.'"

May I and all sentient beings swiftly attain the eradication of the ten evil deeds, the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, perversions, the slandering and disparaging of the Triple Gem, and the sins of icchantikas accumulated over immeasurable kalpas.
"Furthermore, one should reflect:
'The nature of such offenses arises solely from a false and inverted mind; it has no fixed reality that can be apprehended, for it is fundamentally empty and quiescent.'"
"May I and all sentient beings swiftly reach the fundamental source of the mind and forever extinguish the roots of sin.
Next, one should further make the vow of exhortation:
"I pray that all Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions who have not yet attained perfect enlightenment may swiftly attain perfect enlightenment."
"If you have already attained perfect enlightenment, I pray that you will remain forever in the world, turning the wheel of the true Dharma, and not enter into nirvana.
Next, one should further make a vow of sympathetic joy:

"May I and all sentient beings ultimately and forever abandon the mind of envy; regarding all merits cultivated and studied, as well as those already accomplished, throughout all lands in the three periods of time, I rejoice in them all."
"Next, one should further give rise to the vow of dedication:
'May all the merits I have cultivated benefit all sentient beings alike, so that they may together proceed toward Buddha-wisdom and reach the city of Nirvana.'"
Having thus made this vow of dedication, one should again go to another quiet room, sit upright with a single-minded focus, and either recite or silently contemplate my name.
One should reduce sleep; if drowsiness and lethargy are prevalent, one should circumambulate and recite within the practice hall.

Furthermore, when it reaches the time of night, if there are lamps or candles providing light, one should likewise reverently make offerings at the three periods of the day, repent of transgressions, and make aspirational prayers.
If one is unable to perform the rite of light, one should simply remain in another quiet room and recite with single-minded devotion.
One should practice the method of repentance in this manner every day, ensuring that it is never neglected or abandoned.

If a person has a distant foundation of merit from past lives, yet temporarily encounters adverse conditions and commits unwholesome acts, their karmic obstacles will be slight; provided their mind is sharp and their mental power is strong, they shall attain purity after seven days and be freed from all hindrances.
Thus, among these sentient beings, there are differences in the thickness or thinness of their karma and the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, which are immeasurable.
Some attain purity after two weeks; some after three weeks; and others attain purity after as many as seven weeks.
If one has committed various grave offenses with predominant influence in both the past and the present, one may attain purification after a hundred days;
or after two hundred days, or even after a thousand days.

If one possesses extremely dull faculties and the heaviest karmic obstructions, one should simply be able to give rise to a courageous mind, disregarding any thought of cherishing one’s own body or life. One should constantly and diligently recite the name, circumambulate day and night, reduce sleep, perform prostrations and repentance, make vows, and joyfully cultivate offerings, never being indolent or negligent, and not ceasing until death, never withdrawing or retreating.
With such diligence, one will certainly attain purity within a thousand days. "Good son!

If you wish to know the signs of attaining purity, then after seven days have passed from the beginning of your practice, you should, every morning at dawn, place the second wheel-marked seal in your hand and cast it three times in succession."
If one’s body, speech, and mind are entirely virtuous, this is called attaining purity.

Thus, as for all sentient beings of the future who are able to practice repentance, they have each practiced goodness within the Buddha-dharma since the distant past; according to whatever merits they have cultivated, their karma varies in its thickness and thinness, with many such distinctions.
Therefore, when they attain purification, their signs are likewise not uniform.
There may be sentient beings who, upon attaining the complete purity of the three karmas, do not immediately acquire any other auspicious signs.
When certain sentient beings attain the auspicious signs of the three karmas, within a single day and night, they again see light filling their entire room;
or they may smell an extraordinary and exquisite fragrance, such that their bodies and minds feel refreshed and joyful.
Or they may have auspicious dreams, in which they see the Buddha’s physical body coming to bear witness for them; he strokes their head with his hand and exclaims:
"Excellent! You are now pure; I have come to bear witness for you."
"Or one may dream that the body of a Bodhisattva comes to bear witness, or dream that an image of the Buddha emits light to bear witness.

If a person has not yet attained the auspicious signs of the three karmas, but merely first sees or hears such matters as these, they are then false, deceptive, and fraudulent, and are not auspicious signs."

If there are those who have previously cultivated the foundation for supramundane goodness and possess a sharp and vigorous power of concentration, at that time I will manifest my body to them according to their needs for deliverance.
I shall radiate the great light of compassion, causing them to dwell in peace and security, free from all doubt and fear.
Sometimes they manifest various supernatural transformations; sometimes they cause others to remember their own past lives and the deeds they have performed, whether good or evil;
and sometimes, according to their inclinations, they preach various profound and essential teachings.
That person will immediately gain resolute faith in the vehicle they have set out upon, or gradually realize and attain the fruits of the śramaṇa path.

Furthermore, even if those sentient beings are unable to see my transformed body preaching the Dharma, as long as they train with a sincere mind to bring about purity of body, speech, and mind, I shall likewise protect and keep them in mind, causing those sentient beings to swiftly eliminate all manner of obstacles.
The celestial Māra Pāpīyān shall not come to cause destruction; nor shall the ninety-five kinds of heterodox teachers and all ghosts and spirits come to create disorder.
All five hindrances will gradually diminish, enabling them to cultivate the various meditative concentrations and wisdom.

Furthermore, if there are sentient beings in future ages who, though not seeking the path of deliverance through meditative concentration and wisdom, nevertheless encounter various calamities, poverty, suffering, and are oppressed by grief and affliction, they should likewise pay respectful homage, offer worship, and repent for their evil deeds. Constantly making vows, at all times and in all places, they should diligently recite my name with a sincere heart, ensuring that their devotion is genuine.
They shall also swiftly be liberated from various forms of decline and affliction, and after relinquishing this life, they will be reborn in a favorable realm.

Furthermore, in future ages, if there are sentient beings—whether lay or ordained—who wish to receive the pure and sublime precepts but are unable to do so because they have previously committed grave and weighty offenses, they should likewise practice the method of repentance as described above. Once they have attained a sincere mind and achieved the wholesome signs of body, speech, and mind, they may then receive the precepts.

If those sentient beings wish to practice the Mahāyāna path and seek to receive the fundamental bodhisattva precepts of gravity, as well as aspire to receive in their entirety all the prohibitory precepts for both lay and monastic practitioners—

namely, the precept of restraining misconduct, the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas, and the precept of benefiting sentient beings— and yet are unable to find a virtuous and excellent preceptor who has a broad understanding of the Bodhisattva Dharma-treasury;

The practitioner who has previously cultivated [the path] should, with a sincere mind, within the *maṇḍala*, reverently make offerings and look up to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, requesting them to serve as teachers and witnesses.

With single-minded resolve, establish your vow and recite the characteristics of the precepts: first, proclaim the ten fundamental heavy precepts; next, you shall collectively enumerate the three categories of precepts. By vowing and receiving them yourself, you likewise obtain the precepts.

"Furthermore, in future ages, there will be sentient beings who wish to leave the household life, or those who have already left it, but who cannot find a virtuous and excellent preceptor or a pure community of monks.
