At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dṛḍhaśuddhādhimukti addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha, saying:
"How does one reveal and instruct those who seek to advance toward the Mahāyāna regarding the skillful means for their progress?
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha replied,
"O son of good family!
If there are sentient beings who wish to proceed toward the Mahāyāna, they should first know the fundamental practice that must be undertaken at the outset.

This fundamental practice undertaken at the outset consists of cultivating faith and understanding by relying upon the single reality realm (*ekasatya-dhātu*); because the power of this faith and understanding increases, they will swiftly enter the lineage of the Bodhisattvas.

That which is called the realm of the single reality refers to the essence of the sentient beings' mind, which from the very beginning is neither born nor extinguished, pure by nature, unobstructed and unhindered, just like empty space.

Because it is free from conceptual discrimination, it is equal and all-pervasive, reaching everywhere without exception; it fills the ten directions, is ultimately of one single mark, non-dual and undifferentiated, neither changing nor altering, without increase and without decrease.

Because the minds of all sentient beings, the minds of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the minds of all bodhisattvas, and the minds of all buddhas are all identical in being neither arising nor ceasing, undefiled and quiescent, for they possess the characteristic of true suchness (tathatā).
Why is this so? All minds that give rise to discrimination are like magical illusions; they possess no fixed reality.

That which is called consciousness, sensation, perception, mental formations, recollection, conceptualization, cognition, and so forth—these various mental factors are neither blue nor yellow, neither red nor white, nor are they of variegated colors. They have no length or shortness, nor squareness, roundness, largeness, or smallness.
Even if one were to search throughout all worlds as far as the limits of space in the ten directions for the shape or form of the mind, not a single distinct portion could be found.

It is only due to the causes and conditions of the habitual perfuming of sentient beings' ignorance and deluded darkness that false objects appear, causing them to give rise to thoughts of attachment.

It is said that this mind cannot know itself; yet it falsely claims to exist, giving rise to the notion of cognition, calculating "self" and "what belongs to self," while in reality there is no such notion of cognition.
Because this deluded mind ultimately has no substance and cannot be perceived;
if there were no cognizing subject capable of discrimination, then there would be no differentiated characteristics of all realms throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Because all phenomena cannot exist of themselves, but exist only through the conceptual discrimination of the deluded mind.
That is to say, all objective realms are each distinct; one conceives of them as existing, knowing this as "self" and that as "other."
Therefore, all phenomena cannot exist of themselves and thus possess no inherent distinction.

It is solely due to the deluded mind—which fails to know and fail to understand that they are internally non-existent—that one perceives external objects before oneself. Consequently, one falsely gives rise to various conceptualizations of phenomena: thinking they exist or do not exist; thinking "that" or "this"; thinking "right" or "wrong"; thinking "good" or "evil," and so forth, until one falsely generates immeasurable and boundless conceptualizations of phenomena.
One should understand it thus: all phenomena arise from false conceptualization, taking the deluded mind as their basis.

However, because this deluded mind lacks any intrinsic nature (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), it also exists in dependence upon objects; that is to say, it is called "mind" because it perceives and cognizes preceding objects through conditioned thought.

Furthermore, although this deluded mind and the aforementioned objects mutually depend upon one another and arise without temporal sequence, this deluded mind is able to serve as the primary source of all objects.
Why is this so? It is because, based on the deluded mind, one fails to realize that the dharma-realm is of a single characteristic; therefore, it is said that the mind possesses ignorance.
Due to the causal power of ignorance, delusive objects manifest.
Furthermore, it is because ignorance ceases that all objective realms cease; it is not by depending on the objective realms themselves.
Because one does not understand for oneself, one says that objective realms exist.
Furthermore, ignorance does not arise by depending upon objects,
for all Buddhas do not give rise to ignorance regarding any object.
Furthermore, because one does not rely on the cessation of objects, the mind of ignorance ceases.
This is because all objects, from the very beginning, have been self-extinguished by their own essential nature and have never truly existed.
For this reason, it is said that all phenomena have the mind as their fundamental basis.
One should know that all phenomena are collectively termed "mind," because their meaning and essence are not distinct, and they are subsumed within the mind.
Furthermore, all phenomena arise from the mind, manifest as its characteristics, and exist through their conjunction; they arise together and perish together, equally lacking any abiding.

Because all objective spheres merely follow what the mind takes as its object and continue in an uninterrupted succession from moment to moment, they are maintained and exist for a temporary duration.
"The meaning of 'mind' as thus explained has two aspects."
What are these two? First, the internal characteristic of the mind; second, the external characteristic of the mind.
As for the internal characteristic of the mind, it is further divided into two kinds.
What are these two? First is the Real, and second is the Delusive.

That which is called "Real" refers to the fundamental nature and characteristic of the mind: it is suchness without variation, pure and perfect, unobstructed and unhindered, subtle and secret, difficult to perceive; because it pervades all places, it is eternal and indestructible, for it establishes and brings forth all phenomena.

What is called "falsehood" refers to such activities as the arising of thought, discrimination, cognition, mental engagement, and recollection; although these continue in succession and can give rise to all manner of objective realms, they are internally hollow and deceptive, lacking any reality because they cannot be perceived.

What is called "phenomena external to the mind" refers to the various objects and realms of all dharmas; because these objects manifest before one according to whatever is being contemplated, one knows there is a distinction between the internal mind and the external mind.
Thus you should understand: internal false conceptualization constitutes the cause and the essence;
external false appearances constitute the effect and the function.
Based on these meanings, I say that all dharmas are collectively termed "mind."

"Furthermore, you should know that external appearances apart from the mind are like the various objects seen in a dream; they are merely constructed by mental perception and lack any real external reality."
All objective realms are likewise thus, for they are all produced by the deluded imaginings of what is seen in the dream-like consciousness of ignorance.

Furthermore, one should know that because the internal mind does not abide from moment to moment, all perceived and conditioned objects also do not abide from moment to moment following the mind; that is to say, because the mind arises, various phenomena arise, and because the mind ceases, various phenomena cease.
The characteristics of arising and ceasing exist only as names; in reality, they cannot be apprehended.
This is because the mind does not go out to reach the objective realm, nor does the objective realm come in to reach the mind.
Like a reflection in a mirror, there is neither coming nor going.
Therefore, if one seeks a fixed characteristic of arising and ceasing within all phenomena, it is utterly unattainable.
This is because all phenomena are ultimately without substance; they are primordially and eternally empty, for in reality they neither arise nor cease.

If all phenomena are thus truly without arising or ceasing, then there are no signs of differentiation among any objects; they are quiescent and of a single flavor, which is termed *tathatā* (suchness), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and the intrinsically pure mind.
That intrinsically pure mind is serene and perfect, because it is devoid of discriminative characteristics.
That which is devoid of discriminative characteristics is omnipresent, being present in all places.
That which is omnipresent is so called because it serves as the support and basis for the establishment of all phenomena.
"Furthermore, that mind is named the Tathāgatagarbha; it is said to be fully endowed with the karma of immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and untainted pure merits."

Because the Dharma-body of all Buddhas, from the beginningless limit of time, is unobstructed and unimpeded, sovereign and imperishable, its various manifested activities and meritorious deeds are constantly blazing forth, never ceasing.
This means that throughout all worlds, they manifest various activities for the sake of providing diverse transformations and benefits.
With a single Buddha-body, there is the body of all Buddhas.
The bodies of all Buddhas are, in fact, the body of a single Buddha.
All their activities are likewise identical, being characterized by non-discrimination; they do not conceive of "self" and "other," for they are equal and non-dual.
Because they function by relying on the single nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), being identical to spontaneous transformation and having no difference in essence;
thus, the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas pervades all places, remaining perfectly still and unmoving, and constantly acts as a support for sentient beings as they die here and are born there.

It is like space, which can entirely contain all material forms and their various types; for all material forms and their various types exist by depending upon space, being established and brought to growth therein.
Abiding in empty space, it is subsumed within the sphere of empty space.
Taking empty space as its essence, there is nothing that can transcend the boundaries of the realm of empty space.
One should know that within all forms and appearances, the realm of empty space is indestructible.
When the forms and appearances finally perish, they return to empty space.
Yet this fundamental realm of empty space neither increases nor decreases; it is unmoving and unchanging.
The Dharma-body of all Buddhas is likewise: it is able to contain and receive the various karmic retributions of all sentient beings.
Because the various karmic fruits and retributions of all sentient beings are all established and grow in dependence upon the Dharma-body of the Buddhas;
abiding within the Dharma-body, they are encompassed by the sphere of the Dharma-body.
Taking the Dharma-body as its essence, there is nothing that can transcend the realm of the Dharma-body.
"One should know that within the bodies of all sentient beings, the Dharma-body of the Buddhas is likewise indestructible."
When afflictions are severed and destroyed, they return to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
This fundamental realm of the Dharma-body neither increases nor decreases; it is immovable and unchanging.
However, since beginningless time, it has coexisted with the mind of ignorance; through the power of habitual perfuming caused by the conditions of delusion and darkness, false objects appear.

Because they rely on the causal conditions of the habitual perfuming of false objects, a mind associated with conceptual construction arises; they reckon in terms of "self" and "what belongs to self," accumulate various karmas, and undergo the suffering of birth and death—this state of their *dharmakāya* is called "sentient beings."

If, among such sentient beings, those whose dharma-body熏習 (perfuming) is powerful gradually thin their afflictions, become able to weary of the world, seek the path to nirvana, take refuge with faith in the single reality, and cultivate the six pāramitās and all other factors conducive to enlightenment, they are called bodhisattvas.
If, among such bodhisattvas, one fulfills the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas and ultimately attains liberation from the sleep of ignorance, they are further designated as a Buddha.
One should know that such distinctions as "sentient beings," "bodhisattvas," and "buddhas" exist only through reliance on worldly conventional designations;
yet the essence of the dharmakāya is ultimately equal, devoid of any differing characteristics.
“Good son! This is called a brief explanation of the meaning of the realm of the single reality.
If one wishes to cultivate faith and understanding based upon this realm of the single reality, one should train in two kinds of contemplative paths.”
What are these two? First is the contemplation of mind-only consciousness; second is the contemplation of true suchness.

Regarding the study of the contemplation of mind-only consciousness: at all times and in all places, one should observe every action performed by body, speech, and mind, knowing that they are nothing but the mind.

Furthermore, regarding all objects of experience, if the mind dwells upon them with mindfulness, one should examine and know them all, ensuring that the mind does not wander toward indeterminate objects (avyākṛta) without self-awareness.
In every moment of thought, one should observe them all.
Whatever object the mind attends to, one should cause the mind to follow that very object, so that the mind knows itself.
One should know that these mental conceptions arise spontaneously from within one's own mind; it is not the case that all objective realms possess thought or discrimination.

What is meant is that within the inner mind, there spontaneously arise views of long and short, good and evil, right and wrong, gain and loss, decline and profit, existence and non-existence, and so forth—an immeasurable variety of such conceptions.
Yet, regarding all objects of perception, one should never give rise to conceptualization or engage in discrimination.

One should know that because all objects of perception are inherently devoid of discriminative thought, they are themselves neither long nor short, neither good nor evil, and so on, up to being neither existent nor non-existent, transcending all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Observing in this way, one sees that all phenomena arise solely from the mind’s perceptions.
Were it otherwise, apart from the mind, not a single phenomenon nor a single perception could manifest its own distinct characteristics.
One should always maintain such mindfulness within the internal mind, knowing that there are only deluded thoughts and no real objective realm, and not allow this practice to cease or be abandoned.
This is called the cultivation and study of the contemplation of consciousness-only.

If the mind is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and does not know its own mental states, one merely perceives external objects before oneself; this is not called the contemplation of mind-only consciousness.
Furthermore, when one maintains mindfulness of the internal mind, one then knows thoughts of greed, thoughts of hatred, as well as thoughts of delusion and false views.
One knows what is wholesome, what is unwholesome, and what is indeterminate; one knows the mental anxieties and the various sufferings [thereof].
While sitting, according to whatever the mind takes as its object, one contemplates and knows from moment to moment that it is only the mind that arises and ceases.
For example, like the flow of water or the flame of a lamp, there is no abiding for even a moment.
From this, one shall attain the Samādhi of the Stillness of Form.
Having attained this samādhi, one should next train in faith in the contemplation of the mind through śamatha, as well as faith in the contemplation of the mind through vipaśyanā.

One who practices śamatha through the contemplation of the mind cultivates faith by reflecting that the internal mind has no visible characteristics; it is perfectly complete and immovable, neither coming nor going, unborn by its very nature, and free from conceptual discrimination.
One who practices the contemplation of the mind through the cultivation of faith visualizes internal and external forms as arising with the mind and ceasing with the mind;
even when practicing until one visualizes the form-body of the Buddha, it is likewise the same.
Arising with the mind and ceasing with the mind, it is like an illusion, like a magical transformation, like the moon reflected in water, or like an image in a mirror.

It is not the mind, yet it is not separate from the mind; it neither comes nor does it not come; it neither goes nor does it not go; it neither arises nor does it not arise; it neither acts nor does it not act.
“Good son! If one can practice and cultivate faith in these two contemplations of the mind, one will swiftly attain entry into the path of the One Vehicle.
You should know that such ‘contemplation of mind-only consciousness’ is called the gateway to supreme wisdom.”

This is because it enables the mind to become sharp and intense, increases the power of faith and understanding, allows for swift entry into the meaning of emptiness, and brings about the arousal of the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta.

If one studies the true contemplation of suchness, one should contemplate that the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished, does not abide in seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, and is forever free from all conceptualizations of discrimination.

Gradually, one is able to transcend the meditative states and their objective signs of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, thereby attaining the semblance of the samādhi of emptiness.
When one attains the samādhi of similar emptiness, the coarse marks of discrimination regarding consciousness, perception, feeling, and formations do not manifest before one.

Training from this point onward, one is protected and nurtured by spiritual friends who possess great compassion; therefore, being free from all obstacles, one practices diligently without ceasing, and is able to enter progressively into the samādhi of mental tranquility.
Having attained this samādhi, one is then able to enter the *ekavyūha-samādhi*.
Having entered this *ekavyūha-samādhi*, one beholds countless Buddhas, gives rise to a mind of profound and vast practice, and abides in the stage of firm faith.
That is to say, regarding the two paths of contemplation—śamatha and vipaśyanā—one possesses decisive faith and understanding, and is able to resolutely advance toward them.
Whatever worldly meditative concentrations (dhyāna-samādhi) one practices and studies, one remains free from attachment and craving for them.

Furthermore, by universally cultivating all roots of goodness and factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), one is without fear or dread within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and takes no pleasure in the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

This is because one relies upon the most wondrous and skillful means of the mind that practices and inclines toward the two contemplations (*dvividha-vipaśyanā*); for this is the basis of all wisdom and the root of practice.
"Furthermore, there are two types of persons among those who practice and study with the aforementioned faith and understanding. What are these two?
First, those of sharp faculties; second, those of dull faculties."

Those of sharp faculties have already been able to know that all external objects are merely the products of the mind, deceptive and unreal, like dreams or illusions, and they possess absolute certainty free from doubt.
Those whose hindrances are slight and whose distracted minds are few should immediately study the true contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness).

As for those of dull faculties who have not yet realized that all external objects are merely mind— being deceptive and unreal— and whose attachments are deep, whose obscurations arise frequently, and whose minds are difficult to subdue, they should first study the contemplation of mind-only consciousness.
"If a person, though they study and cultivate such faith and understanding, has roots of goodness and karma that are meager and is unable to advance,
their various evil afflictions will not be gradually subdued."
Their minds were filled with doubt and timidity; they feared falling into the three evil realms or being born in the eight states of no leisure.
They feared that they would not constantly encounter Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, and thus fail to make offerings or hear and receive the True Dharma.
Fearing that faith in bodhi is difficult to accomplish,
those who harbor such doubts and fears, as well as various obstacles, should at all times and in all places constantly and diligently recite and remember my name.

If one attains single-mindedness, one's roots of goodness will increase and one's resolve will become sharp and powerful; one should then contemplate that my Dharma-body, as well as the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas, are identical in essence to one’s own body—equal in nature, non-dual and undifferentiated, unborn and unceasing, eternal, blissful, self, and pure, with perfected merit and virtue, and thus worthy of taking refuge in.

Furthermore, one observes the characteristics of one's own body and mind as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure; they are like illusions and transformations, and thus should be reviled and renounced.
If one can practice and study such contemplation, the mind of pure faith will swiftly increase, and all obstacles will gradually diminish. Why is this?
This person is called one who trains in hearing my name, and is also able to train in hearing the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions;

one who is called a student of those who train in wholeheartedly prostrating to and making offerings to me, and is also able to train in wholeheartedly prostrating to and making offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions;
and one who is called a student of those who train in hearing the profound Mahāyāna sūtras.
They are called those who study upholding, copying, making offerings to, and revering the profound Mahāyāna sūtras;
they are called those who study receiving, maintaining, reading, and reciting the profound Mahāyāna sūtras;
they are called those who study remaining far removed from false views and do not fall into slander regarding the profound and true meaning.
They are called those who have faith and understanding in the study of the ultimate, profound, and supreme true meaning;
they are called those capable of eliminating all karmic obstacles;
and they are called those who shall attain an immeasurable mass of merit.

When this person relinquishes the body, they shall never fall into the evil realms or the eight difficult conditions; they will again hear the True Dharma, practice with faith, and will also be able to be reborn according to their vows in the pure Buddha-lands of other directions.

"Furthermore, if a person wishes to be born in a pure Buddha-land currently existing in another direction, they should single-mindedly recite and keep in mind the name of the Buddha of that world, with focused attention and without distraction."
Those who observe in this manner will certainly be reborn in the pure land of that Buddha; their roots of goodness will increase, and they will swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression.
You should know that among all roots of goodness, the practice of single-mindedly focusing the mind on contemplating the equal Dharma-body of all Buddhas is the most supreme karmic deed.
What is called "diligent cultivation" is that which gradually enables one to incline toward the *ekavyūha-samādhi*.

If one reaches this *ekavyūha-samādhi*, then one accomplishes a vast and subtle mind of practice, which is termed "attaining the semblance of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
Because they are able to hear my name, they are also able to hear the names of all the Buddhas of the ten directions;
because they are able to worship and make offerings to me with a sincere heart, they are also able to worship and make offerings to all the Buddhas of the ten directions with a sincere heart.

Because they are able to hear the profound Mahāyāna sūtras; because they are able to uphold, transcribe, make offerings to, and revere the profound Mahāyāna sūtras; and because they are able to receive, maintain, read, and recite the profound Mahāyāna sūtras.

Because they are able to give rise to no fear regarding the ultimate, profound, and supreme true meaning; because they remain free from disparagement; and because they attain a mind of right view and are capable of faith and understanding.
This is because it definitively eliminates all karmic obstructions and brings about the direct realization of an immeasurable mass of merit. Why is this so?
It is because the non-conceptual bodhicitta manifests as tranquil wisdom, giving rise to the activity of skillful means through various vows and practices.
Those who are able to hear my name shall attain the practice of resolute faith and its benefits;
even all those who are capable [of this] shall attain the cause for non-retrogression in the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna).
If one’s mind is distracted and defiled, even though they may recite my name, it cannot be called "hearing" [the Dharma].
Because they are unable to give rise to resolute faith and understanding, they obtain only mundane rewards of merit, and fail to attain vast, profound, and wondrous benefits.
With such a confused and defiled mind, whatever wholesome deeds one may practice will all fail to yield profound and great benefit. "Good son!
You should know that those who diligently cultivate and train in signless dhyāna as described above will, before long, be able to obtain profound and great benefits and gradually become Buddhas.
"Profound and great benefits" refers to attaining entry into the stage of firm faith (*adhimukti*) by accomplishing patient acceptance through faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*).
They enter the stage of the firm dharma-position because they have accomplished compliant patience (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*).
They enter the stage of correct reality because they have accomplished the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, those who have accomplished patient acceptance through faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*) are able to act as the lineage of the Tathāgatas.
One who has accomplished the patience of conformity (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*) is able to understand the conduct of the Tathāgata;
one who has accomplished the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) attains the activity of the Tathāgata.
Regarding those who gradually become Buddhas, there are briefly four types.
What are the four? First, one becomes a Buddha by fulfilling the dharma of faith.

That is to say, based on the stage of the lineage (gotrabhūmi), one possesses decisive faith that all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, pure and equal, and thus free from anything to be wished for or sought.
Second, one becomes a Buddha by understanding the fulfillment of the Dharma.

That is to say, based on the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), one deeply understands the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); knowing that the activities of the Tathāgata are neither created nor performed, one does not give rise to dualistic notions regarding saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, because the mind is free from fear.
Third, one becomes a Buddha by virtue of having realized the perfection of the Dharma.
That is to say, based on the Ground of Pure Mind, one attains the non-conceptual wisdom of the tranquil Dharma and inconceivable, spontaneous karma, because there is no thought of seeking.
Fourth, one becomes a Buddha because all meritorious practices are fulfilled;
that is to say, by relying on the ultimate stage of a Bodhisattva, one is able to eliminate all obstructions, for the dream of ignorance has come to an end.
"Furthermore, you should know that there are three types of those who practice the worldly dhyāna with signs (*sanimitta*).
What are these three?

First, because they lack the power of skillful means and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), they greedily grasp at the merits of various dhyānas and samādhis, giving rise to arrogance; thus bound by their dhyāna, they regress and seek the worldly realm."

Second, because they lack the power of skillful means and resolute conviction, they rely on meditative concentration to give rise to a practice of partial revulsion and detachment; thus, fearing and shrinking from birth and death, they fall back into the two vehicles.

Third, there is the power of skillful means and resolute belief (*adhimukti-bala*), which refers to relying upon the single reality realm (*eka-tattva-viṣaya*) and practicing the two paths of contemplation—*śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*—thereby being able to believe and resolve that all phenomena arise solely from the mind’s perceptions, like dreams and illusions.

Although they attain the various merits of worldly meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), they do not cling to them firmly, nor do they regress to seek the fruits of the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*).

Furthermore, because they trustfully know that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself nirvāṇa, they are neither terrified nor daunted, nor do they regress to seek the vehicles of the two [lesser] vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*).

"One who trains in this manner in all the dharmas of dhyāna and samādhi should know that there are ten sequential gateways of characteristics which fully encompass the practice of meditative concentration, enabling the practitioner to achieve realization in accordance with the truth, without error or deviation."
What are the ten? First, the characteristic of the skillful means for gathering mindfulness.
Second, the characteristic of the desire to abide in the objective sphere.
Third, in the initial stage of abiding, one clearly and distinctly knows the characteristics of exiting and entering the realm.
Fourth, by skillfully abiding in the realm, one attains the characteristic of firm stability.
Fifth, the characteristic of further seeking progress through the application of courageous effort in one's contemplative practice.
Sixth, the characteristic of self-comforting through gradually attaining pliancy, experiencing joy according to one's heart, and removing doubt through resolute faith and understanding.
Seventh, the mark of attaining superior progress: that which the mind is devoted to corresponds even slightly, and one perceives the signs of its benefit.
Eighth, the mark of the accomplishment of antidotes: through further cultivation, practice becomes increasingly clear and firm, and one attains superior merit.
Ninth, the mark of being unerring and unfailing: whatever the mind intends or undertakes, external manifestations of merit correspond to one's wishes.

Tenth, if one practices further in another way, relying on what was previously attained to initiate skillful means, one will achieve successive accomplishments, attaining mastery over entering and emerging at will, characterized by the freedom of transcendence.
"This is called the tenfold sequential gateway of characteristics, which encompasses the practice of meditative concentration.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Firm Pure Faith asked the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha:
"How is it that you skillfully expound the profound Dharma, enabling sentient beings to become free from timidity and weakness?"
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha said: "Good son!

You should know that those who have newly begun their practice and resolved their minds to seek the Mahāyāna, yet have not yet attained faith, will often give rise to doubt and timidity regarding the profound Dharma of the unsurpassed path."

I constantly employ skillful means to proclaim and manifest the true meaning in order to comfort them, causing them to abandon timidity and weakness; for this reason, I am called the One Who Speaks with Skillful Consolation.
What is meant by "consoling"?

It refers to sentient beings of dull faculties and small minds who, upon hearing that the Unsurpassed Way is most supreme and most wondrous, feel a longing for it in their hearts and resolve to set out toward it.

Furthermore, one who contemplates and seeks the unsurpassed path must necessarily accumulate merit to the utmost extent and undergo difficult practices and asceticism; by delivering oneself and others through vast eons, enduring diligent suffering within the cycle of birth and death for a long time, only then can it be attained.
For this reason, a sense of cowardice and weakness arose in his mind.

I then explained to him the meaning of ultimate reality: that all dharmas are by their very nature empty; they are ultimately without self, without agent, and without recipient; they are without self and without other; they are without action and without arrival; they have no location or direction, nor do they exist in the past, present, or future.
He further taught them the eighteen kinds of emptiness and so forth, explaining that among all dharmas—whether saṃsāra or nirvāṇa—there is no truly real characteristic that can be apprehended.

Furthermore, he taught that all dharmas are like illusions and transformations, like the moon in water, like images in a mirror, like a city of the gandharvas, like echoes in a valley, like a mirage, like bubbles, like dew, like a lamp, like the optical defect of *timira*, like a dream, like lightning, and like clouds.
The nature of afflictions and birth-and-death is extremely subtle and weak, making them easy to extinguish.
Furthermore, afflictions and birth-and-death ultimately lack any substantial essence; they cannot be found when sought.
Originally unborn, it is truly without cessation;
its self-nature is quiescent, which is itself nirvāṇa.
What has been thus explained can shatter all views, for by diminishing the conceptual attachments of one’s own body and mind, one attains freedom from cowardice.
"Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, failing to understand the intended meaning of the Tathāgata’s speech, give rise to timidity and weakness.

You should know that the intended meaning of the Tathāgata’s speech is as follows: because the Tathāgata perceives that single reality-realm (*ekasatya-dhātu*), he has ultimately attained liberation from all evil phenomena such as birth, old age, sickness, and death; he has realized that Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is a mass of immeasurable virtues such as permanence, constancy, coolness, and immutability."

Furthermore, one can clearly perceive that within the bodies of all sentient beings there are always such true, subtle, and pure merits, yet these are shrouded and obstructed by the defilement of the darkness of ignorance, causing them to constantly undergo immeasurable sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death throughout the long night.
The Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion toward this, desiring to cause all sentient beings to be free from all suffering and to collectively attain the ultimate bliss of the Dharmakāya.
That Dharmakāya is a dharma that is non-conceptual and free from thought.
It can only be attained by one who is able to extinguish false consciousness and perceptions, such that no further mental attachments arise.
However, all sentient beings constantly delight in discriminating between and clinging to various phenomena; because of their inverted false imaginings, they undergo birth and death.
Therefore, the Tathāgata, wishing to cause them to abandon such discriminative attachments, teaches that all worldly phenomena are ultimately empty in essence and non-existent.
Even all supramundane phenomena are ultimately empty in essence and non-existent.
To explain this extensively, it is as in the case of the eighteen kinds of emptiness.
Thus it is demonstrated that all phenomena do not depart from the essence of bodhi.

The essence of bodhi is neither existent nor non-existent, neither not existent nor not non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent; it is neither one nor different, neither not one nor not different, nor both one and different.
Ultimately, not even a single characteristic can be apprehended, because all characteristics have been relinquished.
To relinquish all characteristics means that they cannot be grasped by relying on verbal expression.
This is because within the Dharma of Bodhi, there is neither one who receives verbal expression nor one who is able to express it.
Furthermore, it cannot be known by relying on mental recollection.
This is because within the Dharma of Bodhi, there is nothing that can grasp and nothing that can be grasped; there is no self and no other, as it is free from conceptual discrimination.
If there is conceptual discrimination, it is then false and cannot be called "correspondence.

Regarding such teachings as these, those of dull faculties who cannot understand them claim that the unsurpassed path and the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body are merely empty dharmas, exclusively and ultimately non-existent; their minds are timid and weak, fearing they will fall into a state of nothingness.
Some give rise to the notion of annihilation and form views of increase and decrease; they further engage in slander, disparaging themselves and belittling others.
For them, I preach that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is by nature not empty, possesses a true essence, and is fully endowed with immeasurable pure merits and deeds.
From beginningless time, it has been spontaneously perfect, neither cultivated nor contrived.
Even within the bodies of all sentient beings, it is fully present—unchanging and undifferentiated, without increase or decrease.
Such teachings as these are able to remove cowardice and weakness; this is called "consolation.
Furthermore, even sentient beings who are foolish and stubbornly attached may experience cowardice and weakness upon hearing such teachings.

Because they grasp at the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body as being inherently complete, characterized by neither cultivation nor fabrication, they give rise to the notion of non-attainment and become timid and weak; or, calculating it to be spontaneous, they fall into perverse and inverted views.
I then taught him to practice all wholesome dharmas, increasing and fulfilling them, so that he might give birth to the form-body of a Tathāgata and attain the pure retribution of immeasurable merit.
Such explanations as these serve to dispel timidity and are thus consoling.
However, the profound meaning I have taught is in accord with reality and is free from all faults, for it is devoid of contradictory statements.
How is it known that one is free from contradictory characteristics?
It is said that within the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata, although there is no realm of verbal expression and it is free from mental conceptions and thoughts, it is neither empty nor non-empty.

Ultimately, there are no marks whatsoever; it cannot be pointed out through verbal expression. Nevertheless, within the context of conventional truth—the realm of illusory transformations, causal conditions, and provisional designations—where things exist in mutual dependence and relation, it can be skillfully manifested and explained.

Because that Dharma-body is in its true nature devoid of discrimination, free from self-characteristics and free from other-characteristics, neither empty nor non-empty, and because it is even remote from all marks, the essence of that Dharma is said to be ultimately empty and non-existent.

Because one is free from mental discrimination, conceptualization is exhausted; there is not a single characteristic that can be seen or known by itself as existing. Therefore, the meaning of emptiness is definitively real, and its correspondence is unerring.

"Furthermore, within that very meaning of emptiness, because one is free from the conceptualizing and deluded mind, there is ultimately not a single characteristic that can be said to be empty; since only the true reality exists, it is therefore non-empty."

Because one is free from the perception of consciousness, there is no mark of any deception whatsoever; it is ultimately eternal, constant, unchanging, and undifferentiated, for there is no further mark that can be destroyed or extinguished, as it is free from increase or decrease.

Furthermore, in that state of non-conceptual reality, because it has been endowed with the natural karma of immeasurable merit since beginningless time, and because it is accomplished in accordance [with that nature]—neither separated from nor detached from it—it is said to be "not empty."

Although all sentient beings possess this collection of substantial entities and virtues, because they are obscured and hindered by the darkness of ignorance, they do not know or see them; unable to realize their virtuous benefits, they are no different from those who have nothing at all, and are thus said to be "non-existent."

Because they do not know or see the essence of those dharmas, all karmic actions consisting of merit and benefit cannot be experienced by those sentient beings; therefore, they are not said to belong to them.

Only by universally cultivating all wholesome dharmas to counteract all obstacles does one perceive that Dharmakāya; thereafter, one attains the benefits of merit. Therefore, it is said that the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas gives rise to the Tathāgata’s form-body and wisdom-body.
“Good son! The profound meaning I have explained is definitive and true, free from the fault of contradiction; you should understand it in this way.

At that time, while the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha was expounding such supreme, skillful, profound, and essential Dharma gates, one hundred trillion sentient beings resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and abided in the stage of firm faith.
Furthermore, ninety-eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The entire great assembly each offered celestial incense and flowers to the Buddha, as well as to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
"Each of you should receive and uphold this Dharma-gate, and wherever you dwell, cause it to be widely disseminated."
Why is this? Because such a Dharma-gate is extremely difficult to encounter and is capable of bringing great benefit.

If a person hears the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha and places faith in what he has taught, you should know that such a person will swiftly be able to leave behind all obstacles and quickly attain the Unsurpassed Way.
Thereupon, the entire assembly spoke with one voice:
"We shall receive and uphold this, disseminate it throughout the world, and dare not allow it to be forgotten.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Firm Pure Faith addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, what is the name of this Dharma-gate within the Sūtra on the Collection of the Six Sense Organs thus spoken?
This is the true essence of the Dharma which I shall receive and uphold, so that all may hear it throughout future ages.”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dṛḍhaśraddhā, saying:
"This dharma-gate is named 'Divination of the Retribution of Good and Evil Karma';
it is also named 'Eliminating All Obstructions and Increasing Pure Faith'."
It is also titled "Revealing the Profound and Ultimate True Meaning through the Expedient Means for Those Seeking and Advancing Toward the Mahāyāna";
it is also titled "The Dharma Gate of Skillfully Consoling and Speaking to Cause One to Leave Behind Timidity and Swiftly Enter Resolute Faith."
"Based on this title and its meaning, you should uphold it.
When the Buddha had finished speaking the name of this Dharma-gate, the entire assembly was filled with joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
